Have you tested this method with large primes?

This math is wrong in 2 ways:

1. Does not change the core problem

/u/0x5f3759df hit on the main reason: completing this algorithm requires knowing all of the factors of an arbitrary number. If that were solvable in the general case then people would just do that to the products involved in RSA encryption, with no need for this algorithm.

On that front, this algorithm does not change the core problem of factoring a prime number and so will not be of any help.

2. Average not generally close to root

For small numbers where the total magnitude of the difference between them cannot be that large (such as in your example), the average and the square root may be fairly close.

However, the average and square root of larger numbers may differ by a much more significant amount:

root( 123456789 * 987654321 ) = 349,188,532

mean( 123456789, 987654321 ) = 555,555,555

diff = 206,367,023

These numbers differ by nearly 60% from the root, and 40% from the mean. This is nowhere near the 4% difference of your example, smaller numbers... and a 60% difference is a very terrible approximation.

I also chose numbers with the same # of digits ("Since in "real life" p and q are about 159 digits (512 bits)") though in algorithm's example they differ in length by 50%.

3. (2 x Prime + 1) is not prime!

However, the biggest problem with this algorithm is that it relies on 2*p+1 being prime if p is prime, and this is simply not the case:

7 is prime. 2*7+1 = 15

15 is not prime.

Therefore, even if this algorithm did run to completion with out the two errors described above, it would not necessarily find prime factors.

Maybe (2n-1) was meant as a formula for finding one prime based off another? That still doesn't help, though, because the exponent n means that you'll be having to find arbitrary (not even square) roots across two variables... what do they call that thing where you have a number, and you need to know what other numbers could multiply together to make it?

Oh, right... factoring. See issue #1.

In Super Mario Galaxy 1 and 2, when you grab the star, there's an animation of Mario grabbing a star, then Mario flying off the level, a few menus popping up, Mario having to go to a place to select another level (less time in SMG2), , a camera panning over the level and then Mario landing. None of this is skippable.

All this can take a bit over a minute in SMG1 and it takes about 40 seconds in SMG2 (but SMG has green stars, many of which take mere seconds to complete). This means that if you want to get all the stars, you'll be waiting to play levels for well over an hour.

The question is, how large amount of that idle time could have been cut out from the game with levels still loading without any problems? Could those idle times that wouldn't have been possible to be reduced still be alleviated somehow? For an example, while the level being loaded, Mario would have been in a small area with at least something to do.

[Video for reference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=haz4uoY2jYA) (starts at 16:54)
